Formulation:
- 19-year-old female college student with acute onset of dysuria and crampy lower abdominal pain, hematuria, and foul-smelling urine, consistent with uncomplicated UTI.
- Predisposing factors: sexually active with new partner, no prior STD screening.
- Precipitating factors: recent onset of urinary symptoms.
- Perpetuating factors: no current treatment, previous ineffective self-treatment with bicarbonate.
- Protective factors: health literacy; understands treatment and when to seek further care.
- Secondary consideration of possible STI due to sexual history but absence of vaginal discharge or typical STI symptoms lowers likelihood.
- IBS history unlikely to explain symptoms given temporal relation to urinary symptoms.

Mental Health Care Plan Details

Principal Problem: Uncomplicated Urinary Tract Infection (Cystitis)
- Patient Goal(s): Resolution of burning urination and abdominal pain; avoid complications
- Clinical Goal(s): Eradicate infection; prevent progression to pyelonephritis; reduce symptom burden
- Actions (Patient):
  • Complete prescribed antibiotic course (Nitrofurantoin or Trimethoprim, 1 tablet twice daily for 3 days)
  • Increase fluid intake
  • Avoid sexual intercourse until symptoms resolve; continue condom use
  • Monitor symptoms and report fever, back pain, or worsening condition
- Actions (Clinician/GP):
  • Prescribe appropriate antibiotic considering allergy to Clindamycin
  • Advise hydration and symptom management (cranberry juice optional)
  • Educate regarding sexual activity during infection
  • Provide clear instructions on when to seek follow-up (e.g., no improvement after treatment or new/worsening symptoms)
  • Arrange further evaluation if symptoms persist beyond one week

Secondary Problem: Possible Sexually Transmitted Infection (Urethritis)
- Patient Goal(s): Rule out STI; maintain sexual health
- Clinical Goal(s): Ensure appropriate screening and management for STIs if indicated
- Actions (Patient):
  • Undergo recommended STD screening
  • Report any development of vaginal discharge or pelvic pain
- Actions (Clinician/GP):
  • Recommend and arrange STD screening tests
  • Counsel on safe sexual practices and need for partner notification/treatment if STI confirmed

Patient Education, Emergency Care & Relapse Prevention:
- Education Given: Yes  
- Topics Covered: Nature of UTI, importance of completing antibiotics, fluid intake, sexual activity advice, symptom monitoring, when to seek further care
- Early Warning Signs of Relapse/Worsening: Fever, flank or back pain, increased urinary frequency or urgency, worsening abdominal pain, hematuria persistence
- Coping Strategies: Hydration, temporary sexual abstinence, adherence to treatment plan

Consent, Coordination & Review:
- Patient Consent to Plan: Implied by participation; explicit consent not documented
- Copy of Mental Health Care Plan Given to Patient: Not recorded (plan oral)
- Other Mental Health Professionals Involved in Patient Care: Not recorded
- GP Acknowledgment (if completed by other MH Professional): Not applicable
- Review Date: Advise follow-up if symptoms persist after antibiotic course (3-7 days post-treatment)

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)
- Uncomplicated Urinary Tract Infection (Cystitis) – High likelihood; classical symptoms of dysuria, suprapubic cramping, hematuria, foul-smelling urine without systemic signs
- Sexually Transmitted Infection (e.g., Chlamydia, Gonorrhea) – Medium likelihood; sexual activity without prior screening, dysuria, hematuria present but no discharge or typical STI symptoms
- Irritable Bowel Syndrome-related Pelvic Pain – Low likelihood; history of IBS but temporal relation and symptoms suggest urinary cause
